rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> one-season (2024-25) RBD field trial on 4-year-old guava, 8 treatments x 3 replications, capacitive soil moisture sensor installed and calibrated, irrigation done manually from sensor readings. Q2: Table 1 and Table 2, Results <U+2013> sensor reduced total water irrigated irrespective of application method (e.g. flood 17965 vs 11396 l/plot; drip 9060 vs 3337 l/plot), irrigation efficiency rose from 25.1% (flood, no SMS) to 89.9% (drip + SMS), and water saving of 28-63% with SMS. Q9: Tables 1 and 2 report SEM and CD(0.05) for water irrigated per plot and for conveyance, field application and irrigation efficiency.
rows.notes: Single method (measured applied water and efficiency ratios), so no triangulation. Soil moisture itself is not reported; Table 1 shows wider intervals and lower frequency under SMS, but this is a component of the applied-water outcome rather than a measured intermediate variable, so Q4 answered no with doubt. One site, one crop, one season, 20 m2 plots; no conditions stated as requirements, no limitations stated. Water-saving percentages themselves have no SEM, but the underlying water-irrigated and IE values do.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own field experiment on guava with sensor and non-sensor treatments.
rows.notes: The study uses a single capacitive soil moisture sensor read manually; irrigation was applied by hand based on readings. There is no app, decision-support software, IoT architecture or automated scheduling, so it provides no evidence on app-based scheduling. What it shows is that manual irrigation guided by a soil moisture sensor reduced applied water and raised irrigation efficiency relative to no-sensor plots.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own field experiment on guava.
rows.notes: No app, IoT or automated scheduling system was tested, and no resilience or risk-management outcome (drought response, yield stability, operational delays) was measured. The study reports only water applied, efficiency, fruit weight/yield and B:C ratio for manual sensor-guided irrigation in one season.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> one-season RBD field trial on guava with SMS vs no-SMS under flood, furrow, sprinkler and drip. Q2: Tables 1-2 and Results <U+2013> SMS-guided plots used less water across all methods and showed higher irrigation efficiency (up to 89.9% for drip + SMS vs 25.1% flood without SMS), with 28-63% water saving. Q9: Tables 1 and 2 give SEM and CD(0.05) for water irrigated and for efficiency measures.
rows.notes: Evidence counts only for the soil-moisture-sensor component of the passage; the study has no IoT architecture, no 'layered' system and does not measure operational delays or user complexity. Sensor readings were used manually. Single method, single site/crop/season, plot scale, no stated conditions or limitations. Q4 no because soil moisture (the intermediate variable) is not reported; interval/frequency data in Table 1 are part of the applied-water outcome.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2013> own field experiment with soil moisture sensor treatments on guava.
rows.notes: The study measures water applied, irrigation efficiency, fruit quality/yield and B:C ratio in a single normal season; it reports nothing on resilience, risk reduction, drought or stress response, or system reliability. No IoT or layered architecture was tested. It therefore provides no own evidence that soil sensors enhance resilience/risk management.

notes: Short single-author paper, full text appears complete. One site (loamy new alluvial soil, sub-tropical West Bengal), one crop (guava cv. Allahabad Safeda), one winter season, 20 m2 plots with two plants each. Statistical dispersion given as SEM and CD in Tables 1-3 but not for water-saving percentages or B:C ratio. No limitations section; some internal inconsistencies (e.g. '553 times' vs '5.53 times').
